section_summary: This section traces postwar efforts to relieve food, clothing, medical, and welfare shortages in occupied Japan, beginning with proposals from Japanese communities in Brazil and petitions from Chinese residents of western Japan. It documents the gradual establishment of approved private-relief channels—especially the Licensed Agencies for Relief in Asia (LARA)—alongside requests for social-work training materials and debates over Japanese food policy, relief appropriations, and the use of Japanese liquid assets. Later records concern relief offers from Argentina and Chile, assistance for Okinawa, and Chinese medical supplies donated to victims of the December 1946 Shikoku earthquake.

keywords: Licensed Agencies for Relief in Asia (LARA)
Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP)

subfiles.title: Japanese Colony in São Paulo Proposal for Relief Shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: American Consulate General, São Paulo
subfiles.about: Reports a proposal by Japanese residents of São Paulo to contribute money, food, and clothing for relief in Japan and requests guidance.
subfiles.summary: Leaders of São Paulo's large Japanese community asked whether they could send relief supplies to Japan, possibly at the rate of one steamer per month. The airgram identifies Kiyoshi Yamamoto and Shigetsuma Furuya as promoters and asks whether the International Red Cross should be used. It also recommends sending current Japanese-language newspapers to counter false reports among Japanese Brazilians that Japan had not actually been defeated.

subfiles.title: Reply Concerning the São Paulo Japanese Relief Proposal
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Advises that the relief proposal has been referred to the occupation authorities in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that São Paulo's proposal was sent to the Acting Political Adviser to SCAP for consideration. It also reports that an inquiry was made about obtaining current Japanese newspapers for distribution in Brazil.

subfiles.title: Inquiry to SCAP on Brazilian Relief Shipments and Japanese Newspapers
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo, for George Atcheson Jr.
subfiles.about: Requests clarification of occupation policy governing relief shipments from Brazil and asks for Japanese newspapers.
subfiles.summary: The Department asks whether food and clothing offered by the Japanese community in Brazil may be imported into occupied Japan and, if so, what approval procedure should be followed. It also endorses the São Paulo consulate's request for newspapers capable of convincing skeptical Japanese Brazilians that Japan had been defeated. Page 5 is the associated mail-section receipt or routing sheet.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Chinese Residents' Petition
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., U.S. Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.to: Walter S. Robertson, American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Chungking
subfiles.about: Forwards a Chinese residents' petition for preferential relief treatment in western Japan.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson encloses a memorandum and a November 16 petition from Chinese residents of western Japan seeking special treatment from the Japanese Government. He suggests that the American Embassy discreetly inform the Chinese Government, while omitting the Political Adviser's internal comments.

subfiles.title: Request of Chinese Residents for Preferential Treatment
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., U.S. Political Adviser
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander and Chief of Staff
subfiles.about: Comments on a petition from long-term Chinese residents of the Kansai region.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum explains that the petitioners represented chiefly long-term Chinese business residents rather than prisoners of war or forced laborers. It notes that many may have accommodated themselves to the Wang Ching-wei regime and offers no specific recommendation. Repatriation is suggested as a development that might soon resolve much of the problem.

subfiles.title: Petition of the Overseas Chinese in the Kansai District
subfiles.from: Li Wan-shih and Pan To-yuen, Delegation of Overseas Chinese in the Kansai District
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Requests food, housing, clothing, communications, education, and repatriation assistance for Chinese residents of western Japan.
subfiles.summary: The petition describes 5,533 Chinese residents and about 20,000 Formosans in the Kansai region, many living in barracks after wartime destruction. It complains of inadequate rations, frozen bank deposits, lack of clothing and bedding, prohibited communications with China, and destroyed Chinese schools. The representatives ask for equal foreign-national rations, additional rice, and assistance returning to China.

subfiles.title: Woman's Association Appeal for Relief to Defeated Countries
subfiles.from: Mildred Waitt, Woman's Association, First Congregational Church of Portland
subfiles.about: Urges that Japan, Germany, and other defeated countries be opened to shipments of food.
subfiles.summary: The Portland church women's association reports that it voted to advocate admitting food shipments to defeated countries. Japan and Germany are expressly named as intended recipients.

subfiles.title: Note on Purchasing Far Eastern Rubber
subfiles.about: Records notification that the United States would purchase allocated natural Far Eastern rubber at a stated price.
subfiles.summary: The note states that standard top grades of natural Far Eastern rubber allocated to the United States would be purchased at 20¼ pence per pound. It appears to be an unrelated or accidentally interfiled record.

subfiles.title: Reply to Mildred Waitt on Relief for Japan and Germany
subfiles.from: Eldred D. Kuppinger for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the current policies governing private food relief for Japan and Germany.
subfiles.summary: The reply says imports into Japan could be approved if occupation authorities considered them necessary to maintain a minimum living standard, although private-relief policy was still pending. Private aid to Germany was unobjectionable in principle but awaited arrangements for distribution through German agencies and registration by the President's War Relief Control Board.

subfiles.title: Inquiry About Christian Science Relief Supplies for Japan
subfiles.from: James Brunot, President's War Relief Control Board
subfiles.to: Eldred D. Kuppinger, Department of State
subfiles.about: Asks whether circumstances permit Christian Science relief supplies to be sent to an Army chaplain in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Christian Science War Relief Committee wished to supply needy Christian Scientists in Japan through a U.S. Army chaplain. The Board had declined authorization because no transmission channel was known, military authorities were understood to be meeting allowable needs, and the Trading with the Enemy Act applied. Brunot asks whether any new developments alter that position.

subfiles.title: Reply to James Brunot on Relief Shipments
subfiles.from: Eldred D. Kuppinger, Department of State
subfiles.to: James Brunot, President's War Relief Control Board
subfiles.about: Confirms that there is no new information permitting relief shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Kuppinger agrees that nothing can yet be added to the Board's explanation to the Christian Science committee. He notes that Tokyo was queried late in 1945 but had not replied and promises to pass along any information received.

subfiles.title: CINCAFPAC Cable on a System for Private Japanese Relief
subfiles.from: CINCAFPAC, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Recommends collecting private relief supplies at a single point for bulk shipment and international distribution in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The cable says offers of food and clothing from any source would be welcome, but small individual shipments presented serious handling difficulties. It recommends consolidated bulk shipments to Japan and distribution by an international organization such as the International Red Cross. The proposal from the Japanese community in Brazil is specifically addressed.

subfiles.title: Instruction to São Paulo Holding Relief Shipments in Abeyance
subfiles.from: Secretary of State
subfiles.to: American Consular Officer in Charge, São Paulo
subfiles.about: Reports that private relief would be welcomed but must await an approved handling and distribution policy.
subfiles.summary: The Department advises that occupation authorities welcome privately contributed relief in principle. Because procedures for handling and distributing it have not been formulated, shipments from São Paulo must remain in abeyance.

subfiles.title: Memorandum Urging Development of Private-Relief Procedures
subfiles.from: Division of Japanese Affairs
subfiles.about: Urges consultation on a method for forwarding and distributing private relief supplies in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum says that establishing a workable procedure for private contributions accords with American traditions. It recommends consulting Mr. Whitman and other officers who had already considered the issue.

subfiles.title: Proposal for a Coordinated Private-Relief Channel to Japan
subfiles.from: Special Projects Division, signed Albert E. Clattenburg
subfiles.about: Proposes coordinated collection, shipping, and distribution arrangements for private relief to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum observes that military authorities welcome relief but have not established the required procedures. It suggests a designated West Coast port, a War Relief Control Board-approved private agency, Army shipping, and distribution by the International Committee of the Red Cross or a mechanism like that used in occupied Germany. It recommends approaching the War Department's Civil Affairs Division, informally or by formal letter.
keywords: International Committee of the Red Cross

subfiles.title: Copy of CINCAFPAC Cable CA 57974
subfiles.from: CINCAFPAC, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Restates the recommendation for consolidated private-relief shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats the February 17 cable welcoming food and clothing while warning against uncoordinated small shipments. It favors collection at one point, bulk transport to Japan, and distribution by an international organization such as the International Red Cross.

subfiles.title: Nominees for the Voluntary-Agencies Mission to Japan
subfiles.from: Fred Atkins Moore and Charlotte E. Owen, American Council of Voluntary Agencies for Foreign Service
subfiles.about: Requests urgent travel clearance for five proposed members of a relief-planning mission to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Council nominates Edward McMahon, Esther B. Rhoads, Leland S. Brubaker, G. Ernest Bott, and Michael J. McKillop. The mission was to proceed quickly to Japan, coordinate with Military Government and Japanese agencies, and return recommendations for future relief services. Immediate State Department clearance is requested.

subfiles.title: Member Agencies of the American Council of Voluntary Agencies
subfiles.from: American Council of Voluntary Agencies for Foreign Service
subfiles.about: Lists the relief, refugee, religious, labor, and social-service organizations belonging to the Council.
subfiles.summary: The printed roster identifies the Council's numerous member and associate agencies. It illustrates the broad voluntary-sector network available for overseas relief and reconstruction programs.

subfiles.title: Reply on the Modified Voluntary-Agencies Mission
subfiles.from: Willard L. Thorp, Department of State
subfiles.about: Explains that the proposed five-person mission had been revised to a three-person study group pending General MacArthur's approval.
subfiles.summary: Thorp notes subsequent conferences among the Council, War Department, and President's War Relief Control Board. The revised plan called for three mission members, one already in Japan, to examine relief problems on terms acceptable to SCAP. Moore would be notified after Tokyo responded.

subfiles.title: Bombay Telegram on Press Reports of Japanese Food Conditions
subfiles.from: Donovan, Bombay
subfiles.about: Reports a Times of India article disputing claims of starvation in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The telegram summarizes a Tokyo despatch by Noyes Thomas headlined that Japan had no starvation and that food stocks were hidden. It also quotes Admiral Fraser as saying he had not observed the reported starvation.

subfiles.title: Church World Service Inquiry About Sending Relief Funds to Japan
subfiles.from: A. Henry Birkel, Church World Service
subfiles.to: Paul F. McGuire, Department of State
subfiles.about: Asks whether funds can be remitted to G. Ernest Bott in Tokyo for relief work.
subfiles.summary: Birkel explains that three Protestant relief bodies had merged as Church World Service and that Fred Atkins Moore was no longer involved. G. Ernest Bott had requested funds in Tokyo, prompting a renewed inquiry about the financial rules for private relief programs in Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply on Procedures for Relief-Fund Remittances
subfiles.from: Paul F. McGuire, Department of State
subfiles.to: A. Henry Birkel, Church World Service
subfiles.about: Reports that procedures for moderate relief remittances to Japan should become effective within a month.
subfiles.summary: McGuire states that procedures were being devised to make moderate transfers for relief purposes unobjectionable. He asks Church World Service to estimate the amounts it expected to remit monthly or annually.

subfiles.title: Congressman Havenner's Inquiry About Relief for a Kobe Orphanage
subfiles.from: Franck R. Havenner
subfiles.about: Requests guidance in answering an inquiry about sending food, clothing, and medicine to a Kobe orphanage.
subfiles.summary: Havenner quotes Gordon K. Chapman of the Presbyterian Board of National Missions, who asks when private relief articles may be sent to Japan. Chapman particularly seeks assistance for a Kobe orphanage housing children whose parents were killed in the bombing. Havenner asks the Department how he should reply.

subfiles.title: Reply to Congressman Havenner Identifying LARA as the Relief Channel
subfiles.from: Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains that LARA is the accredited channel for private relief shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department reports that approved agencies may send supplies for distribution according to need and that Church World Service had already dispatched a shipment. Member agencies of the American Council of Voluntary Agencies had formed LARA, whose representatives were traveling to Japan to finalize distribution arrangements. Gordon Chapman is advised to contact LARA about the Kobe orphanage.

subfiles.title: Conversation on Social-Welfare Materials and a Possible Welfare Commission
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Records discussions with Colonel Nelson B. Neff about educational materials and long-term social-welfare policy for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Neff described Japan's need for social-work literature, training aids, and a durable public-welfare program. Participants agreed that the War Department should coordinate the acquisition and shipment of materials, with assistance from the State Department, Federal Security Agency, and professional groups. A December 12 addendum reports that the War Department found previously assembled materials and would take a more active role; Neff also hoped to explore a social-welfare commission and a SCAP policy statement.

subfiles.title: Request for Social-Work Literature and Training Aids
subfiles.from: Crawford F. Sams, SCAP Public Health and Welfare Section
subfiles.to: Otis E. Mulliken, Department of State
subfiles.about: Requests educational materials to support social-work training and public assistance in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Sams describes a Japanese public-assistance program serving millions of destitute people under the new Daily Life Security Law but hampered by a lack of trained social workers. He requests concise literature on casework, group work, public welfare, social insurance, legislation, child welfare, community organization, and social-work curricula. SCAP was supervising a one-year course for graduates and an in-service program for public-welfare workers, viewing effective welfare administration as a means of strengthening democracy.

subfiles.title: Reply to Crawford Sams on Social-Welfare Assistance
subfiles.from: Otis E. Mulliken, Department of State
subfiles.about: Promises coordinated assistance in obtaining materials for Japan's social-work education program.
subfiles.summary: Mulliken reports that Department officers had discussed the immediate and long-range welfare problems with Nelson B. Neff. The State Department intended to cooperate with the War Department, other federal bodies, voluntary agencies, and professional organizations. He assures Sams of continued interest and welcomes further suggestions.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Approved SWNCC Food Policy Paper
subfiles.from: State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee
subfiles.about: Forwards the approved and amended SWNCC 331/3 food-policy paper for action in the Far Eastern Commission.
subfiles.summary: The Committee reports approval of SWNCC 331/3 at its February 19 meeting, with an amendment identifying the proposed policy as substantially the U.S. policy transmitted to SCAP in 1945. Copies are enclosed, and the State Department is asked to send one to the U.S. member of the Far Eastern Commission.

subfiles.title: Decision Amending SWNCC 331/3
subfiles.from: Secretariat, State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee
subfiles.about: Directs holders to replace a page in the food-policy paper with a revised version.
subfiles.summary: The duplicate copies record the Committee's February 19 approval and amendment of SWNCC 331/3. Holders are instructed to substitute revised page 22 and destroy the superseded page by burning.

subfiles.title: SWNCC 331/3: Food Policy for Japan
subfiles.from: State member and Secretariat, State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee
subfiles.about: Develops a U.S. negotiating position on Far Eastern Commission policy for civilian food relief in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The study analyzes proposed Far Eastern Commission revisions to U.S. food policy, balancing protection of SCAP's authority against Allied concern that Japan not receive preferential access during the world food shortage. It recommends emphasizing Japanese self-help, equitable distribution, maximum domestic production, suppression of black markets and nonfood diversion, and only minimum reliance on imports. Imported food would be justified chiefly to prevent disease or unrest threatening occupation objectives or forces, while no preference should be granted over Allied or liberated populations. The appendix sets out the proposed policy and a U.S. statement defining how SCAP would report needs and how Washington would determine permissible import levels.

subfiles.title: Instructions to the U.S. Member of the Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.from: Ernest A. Gross for J. H. Hilldring, Department of State
subfiles.to: United States Member, Far Eastern Commission
subfiles.about: Authorizes negotiations on Japanese food policy using the approved SWNCC 331/3 position.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum encloses a copy of SWNCC 331/3 and reproduces the amended introductory language. The U.S. member is authorized to negotiate in the Far Eastern Commission on the basis of the paper's conclusions.

subfiles.title: Clara Neely's Inquiry About Gift Parcels to Japan
subfiles.from: Clara J. Neely
subfiles.about: Requests information about sending small bags of food, clothing, and other articles to suffering people in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Neely asks about the collection and mailing of small relief parcels for Japanese recipients lacking food and clothing. She is particularly concerned about missionaries and orphans and asks whether heavy duties would be charged and what procedure should be followed.

subfiles.title: Reply to Clara Neely on Japanese Gift-Parcel Tariffs
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Martin, Department of State
subfiles.about: States that Japan does not levy a tariff on gift-parcel contents and encloses the relevant postal regulation.
subfiles.summary: Martin answers that the Japanese Government was not imposing tariffs on gift-parcel contents. A copy of the U.S. postal regulation defining gift parcels is enclosed.

subfiles.title: Letter to John Taber on Japanese Liquid Assets and Food Imports
subfiles.from: Dean Acheson, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains why Japanese liquid assets should support economic revival rather than be exhausted on food imports.
subfiles.summary: The letter divides Japanese liquid assets into identifiable looted property, unidentifiable looted property, and legitimately held or acquired assets, noting MacArthur's estimate of $275–300 million in total. U.S. policy sought to use nonrestitutable assets for imports needed to accomplish occupation aims. The Department argues that raw materials for reviving export industries would make Japan self-supporting within several years and better protect U.S. taxpayers than spending the assets solely on food.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Statements on Foreign Relief and Japanese Assets
subfiles.from: Dean Acheson, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Sends two statements answering congressional questions about foreign relief and Japanese assets.
subfiles.summary: Acheson encloses statements on foreign-relief programs and on using Japanese liquid assets to buy food. He offers further information and an informal discussion with Taber and his subcommittee.

subfiles.title: Foreign Relief Programs
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes U.S. foreign-relief appropriations, expenditures, programs, and country allocations.
subfiles.summary: The statement estimates combined fiscal-year 1947 and 1948 relief expenditures at $3.447 billion and describes proposed post-UNRRA, occupied-country, and refugee programs. It distinguishes the planned Greek and Turkish assistance from ordinary relief and lists anticipated post-UNRRA recipients. Tables allocate the War Department's requested $1.025 billion among Germany, Austria, Japan including the Ryukyus, and Korea, with $415 million assigned to Japan.

subfiles.title: Use of Japanese Liquid Assets to Purchase Food
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Argues for using nonrestitutable Japanese assets to revive productive industry instead of financing food alone.
subfiles.summary: The statement classifies Japanese liquid assets according to whether they were looted and identifiable, looted but unidentifiable, or legitimately held. It reports MacArthur's valuation and notes that disposal required Far Eastern Commission policy decisions. The Department favors using available assets for raw materials and export recovery so Japan can become self-sustaining rather than consuming the assets on food imports.

subfiles.title: Buenos Aires Inquiry About Japanese Relief Shipments
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Asks whether local Japanese may send food or clothing to Japan and Okinawa and through which agencies.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy requests instructions for the local Japanese community. It asks whether supplies may be sent directly or through the United States and what distributing agencies should be used.

subfiles.title: Airgram to Santiago Identifying LARA as the Approved Relief Agency
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Advises that the Chilean Red Cross should coordinate its proposed Japan shipment through LARA.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that LARA was the only agency recognized by SCAP to receive and distribute relief supplies in Japan. The Chilean Red Cross is directed to contact LARA chairman Edward B. Peacock, and distribution is described as jointly conducted by LARA and Japanese governmental agencies under U.S. military supervision.

subfiles.title: Reply to Buenos Aires on Parcels and Bulk Relief
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Directs Argentine donors to postal authorities for parcels and to LARA for bulk relief shipments.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy is told to consult the Argentine Post Office about gift-parcel service to Japan. Questions about bulk shipments for general distribution should be addressed to LARA chairman Edward B. Peacock. Mail service arrangements were not yet complete.

subfiles.title: Internal Note on Argentine Relief and Parcel-Post Arrangements
subfiles.from: Special Projects Division
subfiles.about: Records War and Post Office Department advice on proposed Argentine shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Colonel Linville said the Argentine Japanese group should ask LARA whether it would accept relief supplies and that the War Department had no objection to an agreed arrangement. Mr. Peterson reported that parcel post could be forwarded through the United States if Argentina packed individual parcels into bulk containers, avoiding separate handling in transit.

subfiles.title: Request for Recommendation on Supplies for the Sacred Heart Convent
subfiles.from: War Department Civil Affairs Division
subfiles.about: Requests a recommendation on a proposed shipment of equipment, bedding, and food to a Tokyo convent.
subfiles.summary: A Pacific trading company wished to send Reverend Mother Britt of the Society of the Sacred Heart blankets, mattresses, trunks, a typewriter, sleeping bags, and approximately one and one-half tons of miscellaneous food. All items were intended for the Sacred Heart Convent in Tokyo, and theater authorities were asked for a recommendation.

subfiles.title: Buenos Aires Follow-up on Bulk Relief for the Ryukyu Islands
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Asks whether bulk relief may now be sent to the Ryukyu Islands under the same rules as shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy cites earlier correspondence on Japanese and Okinawan relief and a notice restoring postal and individual gift-parcel service to the Ryukyus. It asks whether bulk shipments are also permissible and whether Japan's regulations and mails apply.

subfiles.title: Reply Authorizing Bulk Relief Through LARA
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Advises that bulk relief shipments may be made through LARA.
subfiles.summary: The Department confirms that bulk relief may proceed through LARA. Potential shippers are again directed to Edward B. Peacock for the applicable regulations.

subfiles.title: Chilean Red Cross Inquiry About Relief for Japanese Children
subfiles.from: Claude G. Bowers, U.S. Embassy, Santiago
subfiles.about: Asks how a Chilean Japanese community may send food and clothing to needy children in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Chilean Red Cross had been asked to transmit 100,000 pesos' worth of clothing and food to the Japanese Red Cross for children. Grace Line offered transport to San Francisco, and the Embassy asks whether onward shipment is permitted and what U.S. authorizations are required.

subfiles.title: Chinese Red Cross Medical Supplies for Shikoku Earthquake Victims
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports the transfer of Chinese-donated medical supplies to Japanese victims of the December 1946 Shikoku earthquake.
subfiles.summary: The Chinese Mission in Japan offered about thirty cases of medical supplies and other necessities collected by the Chinese Red Cross and philanthropic organizations. SCAP's welfare section, American and Japanese Red Cross representatives, and the Japanese Welfare Ministry arranged transfer on August 27. Many containers bore U.S. Medical Department, UNRRA, CNRA, or American Red Cross markings and were valued at $4,000–$5,000. Officials questioned the diversion of supplies needed in China, especially after a Chinese hospital in Tokyo requested similar medicines the following day.

subfiles.title: Confidential Transmittal of the Earthquake-Relief Despatch
subfiles.from: William H. McCahon, Department of State
subfiles.to: Philip E. Ryan, American Red Cross
subfiles.about: Confidentially forwards the Tokyo despatch on Chinese Red Cross aid to Japanese earthquake victims.
subfiles.summary: McCahon sends Ryan a copy of despatch 1268 from the U.S. Political Adviser in Tokyo. The enclosed report concerns the Chinese Red Cross contribution for victims of the Shikoku earthquake.

subfiles.title: American Red Cross Acknowledgment and Supply Investigation
subfiles.from: Philip E. Ryan, American Red Cross
subfiles.to: William H. McCahon, Department of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the earthquake-relief report and notes an investigation into the supplies' source.
subfiles.summary: Ryan states that American Red Cross representatives in Tokyo had already reported the Chinese contribution. Its Shanghai representative was investigating the original source of the supplies.

subfiles.title: Argentine Diplomatic Note on a 52-Ton Relief Shipment
subfiles.doc_type: diplomatic note with English translation and Spanish original
subfiles.from: Oscar Ivanissevich, Argentine Ambassador
subfiles.to: Robert E. Lovett, U.S. Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Requests assistance forwarding an Argentine government gift of provisions to Japan and Okinawa through LARA.
subfiles.summary: Argentina's National Executive Committee for Aid to Peoples Affected by the War shipped 52 tons of provisions from Buenos Aires aboard the Fisk Victory on October 14. The gift, made by President Juan Perón in the name of the Argentine people, was destined for Japan and Okinawa via San Francisco. Bills of lading were sent to the Argentine consul for delivery to LARA, and the Ambassador asks U.S. authorities to expedite the transfer and reshipment.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of the Argentine Relief Shipment
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Confirms that arrangements were made to forward Argentina's relief supplies to Japan and Okinawa.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Argentine note D.E. 518 concerning the gift routed through LARA. It reports that appropriate arrangements for forwarding the shipment had been completed.

subfiles.title: Conversation on Arrangements for the Argentine Shipment
subfiles.from: Mrs. Correll, Department of State
subfiles.about: Records confirmation that LARA had already arranged to handle the Argentine relief shipment.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Correll contacted the Advisory Committee on Voluntary Foreign Aid about the Argentine Embassy's October 28 note. Miss Borschke consulted LARA and later reported that it was already coordinating with the Embassy and taking all necessary measures.
